S. are not constitutionally entitled to bond hearings while awaiting deportation. The ruling comes as the Supreme Court prepares to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha this term, a closely related fight over whether the federal mandatory-detention statute applies at all to longtime immigrants arrested inside the country — setting up the possibility that the justices could either undercut Friday’s ruling or strengthen the government's hand. If he wins, Flávio Bolsonaro would secure the eighth consecutive rightist victory in Latin America’s presidential elections, boosting US efforts to influence the region. The son of Brazil’s former president, Bolsonaro has pledged closer ties with Washington and lower public spending — the latter contributing to bullishness that saw markets surge after his first-round victory. Despite relatively low unemployment and solid growth, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s popularity has wilted amid mass debt — partly explaining why both candidates delivered “costly pitches to voters… while saying little about how they’d pay for them ,” Bloomberg wrote. — Brendan Ruberry

Connor Warning: There is a strobe effect in this post. A couple weeks ago I walked into a campus preview screening of Warner Bros.’ Digger . By the time I walked out, the studio heads had been fired. Or the news that they had been fired had reached the trade press. They weren’t fired because Digger was about to flop epically, but they weren’t not fired because Digger was about to flop epically. Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy were the heroes of 2025—they had greenlit the originals Sinners , Weapons , and One Battle After Another —but they were having a terrible 2026. They probably knew they were on the block as soon as Skydance finally managed to acquire Warner Bros. Whether they end up at Netflix or producing on their own, De Luca and Abdy will be fine. Digger , the last movie to come out in their tenure, the last Warner Bros. movie under the pre-Skydance banner, will not. Everyone knows this.

articles.author: By Jessie Blaeser and Erin Doherty
articles.summary: President Donald Trump is asking voters to “pretend” he is on the ballot. That might backfire. New results from The POLITICO Poll show that Democratic midterm voters are more motivated to oppose the president than Republican voters are to support him. Many Republican voters also aren’t looking for blind loyalty to Trump in the midterms: Half say they’d rather their local candidate aim to win, even if it means speaking out against the president. It’s not uncommon for voters in the party out of power to be more motivated in a midterm year. But the lopsided findings are an ominous sign for Trump, who has fundamentally reshaped the GOP over the past decade and has once again staked his brand — and political capital — on delivering wins for Republicans in November. With less than two weeks before the election, the poll suggests Republicans are pragmatic, and care more about preventing a blue wave than standing by Trump. And in a year when voter frustration over high prices appears poised to play a major role, that distinction could prove consequential.
